unit.title: Draw and interpret sketch and simple drawing

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Your team is about to build a staircase frame. The supervisor issues a new revision of the drawing. What should happen to the old copies in the shop?
options: Keep them at the bench as a spare reference
Collect them and mark them void, or destroy them
Give them to the newest trainee to practise on
Pin them up beside the new copy to compare

questions.stem: Where on a drawing would you find what was changed between revision B and revision C?
options: In the parts list, beside each part
On the back of the drawing sheet
Inside the projection symbol box
In the revision table or block

questions.stem: Which drawing would a fitter use to see how all the parts of a steel canopy fit together and where each one goes?
options: The general arrangement (GA) drawing
The detail drawing of one part
The cutting list
The weld procedure sheet

questions.stem: In third angle projection, where is the plan (the view from above) placed?
options: Below the front view
To the left of the front view
Above the front view
Beside the end view, on the right

questions.stem: In first angle projection, where is the view seen from the left of the object drawn?
options: To the left of the front view
Above the front view
To the right of the front view
Below the plan view

questions.stem: A front view shows two thin dashed lines running from top to bottom through a solid steel block. What do they most likely show?
options: A hidden hole through the block
The centre line of the whole block
Where a section view is cut
A weld run on the far side

questions.stem: On a sectional view, why are the hatching lines of two parts that touch drawn in different directions?
options: To show which part is heavier
To show which part is welded first
To show which part is painted
To show that they are separate parts

questions.stem: A size on a drawing is shown in brackets, for example (450). What does this usually mean?
options: It must be held to a much tighter tolerance
It is for reference only, not for working to
It is in inches, not in millimetres
It is the size before welding

questions.stem: A row of holes is dimensioned 100, 100, 100 from each hole to the next (chain dimensions). What is the main risk when making the part?
options: Small errors add up along the row
Each hole will end up too large in size
The drawing is not to scale
The holes must be slotted

questions.stem: A part is dimensioned 250 mm, +0.5 / −0.0. Which measured length is acceptable?
A drawing is at a scale of 1:25. A frame is drawn 64 mm wide. What is its real width?
options: 640 mm

questions.stem: A gate 3.6 m long must fit within 300 mm of drawing space. Which is the largest of these scales that will fit?
On an AWS-style weld symbol, the fillet weld triangle is drawn below the reference line. Which side of the joint is welded?
options: The other side, away from the arrow
Both sides of the joint
Whichever side the welder chooses
The arrow side of the joint

questions.stem: On a weld symbol, the number 6 is written to the left of the fillet triangle. What does it mean?
options: Weld it in 6 runs
A 6 mm fillet leg size
Make 6 welds along the joint
Use a 6 mm electrode

questions.stem: A fillet weld symbol shows 50-150 to the right of the triangle. What does this mean?
options: A weld from 50 mm to 150 mm along the joint
Weld size between 50 and 150 per cent
Welds 50 mm long, spaced at 150 mm centres
A 50 mm gap with 150 mm welds between

questions.stem: What is the tail (the V-shaped end of the reference line) of a weld symbol used for?
options: To give a process or reference note
To show the direction the weld is made in
To show the weld is ground flush
To show where the weld must stop

questions.stem: For a single-bevel butt weld symbol, the arrow has a break (a bend) in it and points to one plate. What does that show?
options: That plate is welded first
That plate is the one to be bevelled
That plate is thinner than the other
That plate must be preheated

questions.stem: A weld symbol has a straight line drawn over it with the letter G beside it. What does this ask for?
options: Grind the weld flush
Gas weld the joint
Gouge the root first
Galvanise after welding

questions.stem: A drawing calls for 'RHS 100 × 50 × 4'. What do the three numbers give?
options: Height, length and number of pieces
Weight per metre, height and grade
Width, length in metres and gauge
Depth, width and wall thickness, mm

questions.stem: A parts list says 'L 75 × 75 × 8'. What is this?
options: A flat bar 75 mm wide and 8 m long
A channel 75 mm deep with 8 mm flanges
An equal angle, 75 mm legs, 8 mm thick
A square tube 75 mm with 8 holes

questions.stem: A note on a gate drawing says 'Hot-dip galvanise after fabrication'. What does this tell the fabricator?
options: Finish all welding and drilling before galvanising
Use galvanised steel and weld it as supplied
Paint the frame with zinc paint before welding
Galvanise the parts first, then weld them

questions.stem: A drawing note says 'Remove all sharp edges'. What should the fabricator do?
options: Grind every edge to a 10 mm radius
Leave edges as cut, unless they are welded
Lightly deburr or chamfer all edges
Cut every corner off at 45°

questions.stem: The drawing shows a bracket where a pipe already runs on site. As team leader, what is the right action?
options: Move the bracket to where it fits and say nothing
Stop, report it and get the change in writing
Cut the pipe away so the bracket fits as drawn
Leave the bracket out and finish the rest

questions.stem: You sketch a damaged bracket on site so a new one can be made. Why should you also take a photo with a tape measure in view?
options: It is quicker to share on social media
It means the sketch needs no sizes at all
It must be taken before any sketch is drawn
It records the shape and checks the sizes

questions.stem: On an isometric sketch, along which lines can true lengths be measured?
options: Along any line, at any angle
Only along the vertical lines of the sketch
Along lines parallel to the axes
Only along the diagonals

questions.stem: Which is the best way to keep a freehand sketch of a long frame in proportion?
options: Draw each part at any size and write the sizes on
Measure each line of the sketch with a steel rule
Use a ruler and draw it exactly to a scale of 1:1
Use grid paper and count squares for each length

questions.stem: To make a cutting list from a frame drawing, why must you know whether the corners are mitred or butted?
options: It changes the cut length of each member
It changes the grade of steel that must be used
It changes which electrodes are used
It changes the paint colour required

questions.stem: A square frame is 1200 mm outside, made of 50 mm square tube with butt corners: two sides full length and two fitted between them. What is the cut length of each fitted piece?
A 600 mm square frame (outside size) is made with mitred corners. What is the cut length of each piece, measured along its outside edge?
options: 550 mm
600 mm
650 mm
500 mm

questions.stem: A hole note reads '6 × Ø14 EQ SP on 120 PCD'. What does 'EQ SP' mean?
options: Equally spaced
Equal size and depth
Extra quality steel plate
Exact position, special

questions.stem: The parts list says 4 off part 7, but the GA drawing clearly shows 6. What should you do?
options: Make 4, because the parts list is always right
Make 5, to be half way between the two
Make 6 and change the parts list yourself
Check with the drawing office or supervisor

questions.stem: On a weld symbol, fillet triangles are drawn both above and below the reference line. What does this mean?
options: Two runs on the arrow side only
A double-sized fillet weld
A fillet weld on both sides
The weld size is not known

questions.stem: Many shops now view drawings on a tablet or phone. What is the main risk?
options: The phone will scale every size for you
The battery may make the sizes change
Tablets cannot show weld symbols at all
Fine detail is easy to misread on a small screen

questions.stem: A cutting plane line on a view is marked A–A, with arrows at each end. What do the arrows show?
options: The direction the part is welded
The way you look to see the section
The direction in which the steel was rolled
Where the part is lifted from

questions.stem: A bracket has a face that slopes at 30°. Why might the drawing include an auxiliary view?
options: To show the true shape of the sloping face
To show the inside of the bracket in section
To show the bracket at a larger scale
To show the bracket after painting

questions.stem: A drawing of a left-hand bracket says '1 off as drawn, 1 off opposite hand'. What does this mean?
options: Make the same part twice, exactly alike
Turn the drawing upside down to read it
Make one as drawn and one mirror image
Weld one from the right-hand side

questions.stem: Which is usually enough to describe a simple flat bracket plate with two holes?
options: One view, with a thickness note added
Four views and an isometric
Plan, front, side and section
An isometric only, with no sizes on it

questions.stem: The title block gives one grade of steel. The store only has a stronger grade of the same size. What should you do?
options: Use it, because stronger steel is always fine
Use any steel of the same size and shape
Stop the job and wait, without telling anyone
Ask the supervisor or engineer to approve it

questions.stem: A long beam is drawn with a zigzag line across it near the middle. What does this mean?
options: The beam must be cut there
Part of the length is left out
The beam is joined by a weld there
The beam is bent at that point

questions.stem: A note says 'Ø22 holes for M20 bolts'. Why is the hole bigger than the bolt?
options: So the bolt can be welded in the hole
So the paint does not fill the hole
To give clearance so the bolts fit
Because drills always cut undersize

questions.stem: A trainee in your team does not understand a section view. What is the best way to help?
options: Tell them to work it out in their own time
Show them the cutting plane and a real part
Do that part of the job for them
Tell them to follow the GA only

questions.stem: Why should drawings marked up in red pen with site changes be handed back to the office after the job?
options: So the master drawings show what was built
So the paper can be recycled by the office
So nobody can see the mistakes made
So the customer pays for the drawings

questions.stem: Three parts, each 200 ± 0.5 mm long, are welded end to end with no gaps. What is the largest possible total length?
After a frame is fabricated, what is the best way to check it against the drawing?
options: Look at it from a distance and compare the shape
Check only the overall length and width
Ask the welder if it was made to the drawing
Measure key sizes and diagonals, and record them

questions.stem: A drawing gives the size of a hexagon nut as 30 A/F. What does A/F mean?
options: Average fit
Across flats
Angle face
After finishing

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: On an AWS-style weld symbol, a fillet triangle drawn above the reference line means the weld is on which side of the joint?
What do the letters BOM stand for on a drawing?
A drawing is at a scale of 1:20. A beam is drawn 145 mm long. What is its real length, in millimetres?
A size is shown as 75 ± 0.25 mm. What is the smallest acceptable size, in millimetres?
What do we call a view drawn as if the part has been cut through, to show its inside shape?
What do the letters CHS stand for in a steel section size?
What is the name of the drawing that shows the shape of a sheet metal part laid out flat, before it is bent or rolled?
A drawing is at a scale of 1:5. How big, in millimetres, is the circle drawn on the paper for a 12 mm hole?
What do the letters UB stand for in a steel beam size, such as 203 × 133 UB 25?
The first hole in a row is 40 mm from the end of a bar, followed by 5 spaces of 80 mm. How far is the last hole from that end, in millimetres?
What is the name of the thin line with an arrowhead at each end that has the size written on it?
What is the name for the thin, evenly spaced lines drawn at an angle across a cut surface in a section view?
What is the name of the groove weld that the 'V' symbol on a weld symbol stands for?
A 50 mm size has a tolerance of +0.2 / −0.1 mm. What is the total tolerance band, in millimetres?
What is the name of the list, kept with a set of drawings, that gives each drawing number and its latest revision?

essays.stem: Explain how you would check a new set of fabrication drawings before your team starts work. Say what you look at on each sheet and why.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check the drawing register, so I know I have every sheet and that each is the latest revision. On each sheet I read the title block: the drawing number, title, revision letter, date, scale, projection symbol, units and who checked and approved it. I read the revision table to see what has changed since the last issue. I read all the notes: material grade, finish such as painting or galvanising, general tolerances, weld notes and any reference to a specification. I compare the GA with the detail drawings and the parts list, checking that part numbers, quantities and sizes agree. I check that the overall sizes add up and look for missing sizes, clashes with site conditions and anything I do not understand. I mark any questions and send them to the supervisor or drawing office before work starts, because a mistake found on paper is cheap to fix, but one found after cutting and welding wastes time and steel.
markingPoints: Checks the register and that every sheet is the latest revision
Reads the title block: number, scale, projection, units, approval
Reads the notes: material, finish, tolerances, weld notes, specifications
Cross-checks GA, details and parts list; sizes add up; looks for clashes and gaps
Raises queries before work starts, and says why (cost of later errors)

essays.stem: Describe how first angle and third angle projection differ, how you would find out which one a drawing uses, and what could go wrong if you mixed them up.
essays.modelAnswer: Both show an object in several flat views, usually the front view, the plan from above and an end view. In first angle projection, each view is placed on the far side of the object from where it is seen: the plan goes below the front view and the view from the left goes on the right. In third angle projection, each view is placed on the same side it is seen from: the plan goes above the front view and the view from the left goes on the left. To find out which is used, look at the projection symbol in the title block, which shows a cone in two views; the position of the circles tells you the method. If you mix them up, you can read a view as the wrong side of the part. Holes, bevels or brackets may then be put on the wrong face or the wrong hand, and a whole batch of parts could be made as a mirror image and scrapped.
markingPoints: Both use several flat views (front, plan, end)
First angle: plan below, left view on the right
Third angle: plan above, left view on the left
Find the method from the projection symbol in the title block
Mixing them up puts features on the wrong face or hand, causing scrap

essays.stem: Explain the parts of an AWS-style weld symbol: the arrow, the reference line, a symbol below or above the line, the size, the length and pitch, the tail, weld-all-round and the field weld flag. Say what each tells the welder.
essays.modelAnswer: The arrow points to the joint to be welded. The reference line is the horizontal line joined to the arrow; all the information is placed on it. A weld symbol drawn below the reference line means the weld is on the arrow side of the joint; above the line means the other side; on both sides means weld both sides. The weld size is written to the left of the symbol, for example 6 for a 6 mm fillet leg. The length and pitch are written to the right: 50-150 means welds 50 mm long at 150 mm centres, and no length means weld the full length. The tail at the end of the reference line holds extra information, such as the welding process, a procedure number or a note. A circle where the arrow meets the reference line means weld all the way round the joint. A flag at that point means the weld is made in the field, on site, not in the workshop. Reading every part correctly makes sure the weld is the right type, size and place.
markingPoints: Arrow points to the joint; information sits on the reference line
Below the line = arrow side, above = other side, both = both sides
Size to the left; length and pitch to the right (with an example)
Tail gives the process, procedure or other notes
Circle = weld all round; flag = field (site) weld

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how you would make a dimensioned sketch on site of an existing steel staircase stringer and landing, so that a replacement can be made in the workshop. Say how you would check the sketch.
essays.modelAnswer: I plan the visit: squared paper, clipboard, pencil, tape, steel rule, spirit level, square, camera or phone, and a team member to hold the tape. I check the area is safe to work in. I study the stair and decide on the views: usually a side elevation of the stringer, a plan of the landing and details of the fixings. I draw the outlines freehand in proportion, using the grid. I then measure and write on the overall rise and going, the number of steps, each step's rise and going, the stringer section size, the landing size and height, and the positions of the fixing holes, all from clear datums such as the finished floor level and the wall face. I note the material, the section sizes, any corrosion, and the condition of the fixings. I take photos with the tape in view. Finally I check the sketch: the step sizes must add up to the overall rise and going, and a second person re-measures the key sizes before we leave.
markingPoints: Plans tools, a helper and safe access
Chooses suitable views (side elevation, plan, details)
Freehand outline in proportion before measuring
Measures and records all key sizes from clear datums, with materials and condition
Checks the sketch: sums agree, photos with tape, second person re-measures

essays.stem: Explain how you would use a GA drawing and detail drawings of a steel frame to produce a cutting list. Include how corner joints affect the cut lengths, and give a worked example.
essays.modelAnswer: I first read the GA to see every member, its part mark and how many are needed, then each detail drawing for the section size, material and end details. I list each part with its mark, section, quantity and cut length. Corner joints change the cut lengths. For example, a frame 1500 mm × 1000 mm outside, made of 50 × 50 mm square tube with butt corners, where the top and bottom run full width, needs 2 pieces at 1500 mm and 2 uprights at 1000 − 2 × 50 = 900 mm. If the corners are mitred, all four pieces are cut to their outside length, so 2 at 1500 mm and 2 at 1000 mm, with 45° ends. I add the saw cut allowance when working out how many pieces come from a stock length. I add up the total length of each section to order the material, and I get a second person to check the list against the drawing before cutting.
markingPoints: Reads the GA for members, marks and quantities, and the details for sections and ends
Lists mark, section, quantity and cut length for each part
Explains butt corners: fitted pieces are shortened by two section widths
Explains mitred corners: outside length with 45° ends; gives a correct worked example
Allows for saw cuts, totals material, and has the list checked

essays.stem: Explain what tolerances are, how they are shown on a drawing, and how they add up when parts are joined. Use an example.
essays.modelAnswer: No part can be made to an exact size, so the drawing gives a tolerance: how far the real size may be from the size drawn and still be accepted. Tolerances can be shown as plus or minus a value, such as 200 ± 0.5 mm; as two different limits, such as 200 +0.5 / −0.0; as the largest and smallest sizes written one above the other; or by a general tolerance note in the title block that covers every size without its own tolerance. When parts are joined end to end, their tolerances add up. For example, three parts each 200 ± 0.5 mm could make a total from 598.5 mm to 601.5 mm, a spread of 3 mm, even though each part is good. This is why important sizes should be measured from one datum, why the designer may give a tight tolerance on the overall size, and why the fitter checks overall sizes during assembly, not only each part.
markingPoints: Defines tolerance as the allowed difference from the drawn size
Shows at least two ways tolerances appear (±, unequal limits, limits, general note)
Explains that tolerances add up when parts are joined
Gives a correct worked example
Links this to datums, overall size checks or design choices

essays.stem: Explain how you would read a structural steel drawing of a beam with end plates and stiffeners: the section size, hole positions, weld details and notes.
essays.modelAnswer: I start with the title block and notes, for the steel grade, finish, bolt grade and general tolerances. I read the beam's section size, such as 203 × 133 UB 25, which gives its depth and width in millimetres and its mass per metre in kilograms, and I check its length and part mark. I then read the end plate details: plate size and thickness, and the hole positions, which are given from datums such as the top of the plate and the centre line, with the hole size and the number of holes. I check the gauge (the distance between hole lines) and the pitch. I read the stiffener sizes and where they go along the beam. I then read the weld symbols for each joint: type, size, which side, and whether it is all round or a site weld. Finally I compare the end plate hole positions with the drawing of the column or bracket it bolts to, to make sure they match.
markingPoints: Reads the title block and notes (grade, finish, bolts, tolerances)
Explains the section size (depth, width, mass per metre), length and part mark
Reads end plate size and hole positions from datums, with gauge and pitch
Reads stiffener positions and every weld symbol
Checks the holes match the connecting member

essays.stem: Explain how drawings should be controlled in a fabrication shop (register, revisions, issue and withdrawal, mark-ups), and the team leader's part in this.
essays.modelAnswer: A drawing register lists every drawing number with its latest revision and the date it was issued. When a drawing is changed, it gets a new revision letter and the change is described in the revision table. The new copy is issued to the people who need it, and the old copies are collected and stamped void or destroyed, so no one can work from them. Copies given out are recorded, so the office knows who must get the next revision. If changes are agreed on site, they are marked up in red on a working copy, signed and dated, and returned to the office so that the master drawing can be updated. The team leader checks the register before work starts, makes sure the team works only from current copies, removes old ones from the work area, records any agreed changes, and reports mistakes or queries to the drawing office. This stops parts being made to an old design and keeps a true record of what was built.
markingPoints: Register lists drawings and their latest revisions
Revisions are lettered and the changes recorded in a table
Issue of new copies and withdrawal of old ones is controlled and recorded
Site changes are marked up, signed, dated and returned to update the master
Team leader checks revisions, removes old copies and reports queries

essays.stem: Compare a freehand sketch, a computer (CAD) drawing and a photograph as ways to pass information about a job to the workshop. Give an advantage and a limit of each.
essays.modelAnswer: A freehand sketch is quick and needs only paper and a pencil, so it can be made on site while you look at the job. It can show sizes, hidden features and notes. Its limit is that it is not to scale and can be untidy or unclear, and sizes may be missed. A CAD drawing is accurate and to scale, easy to change and copy, and can give the exact sizes, cutting lists and weld symbols. Its limits are that it needs a computer, software and a trained person, and it takes longer to make. A photograph shows the real shape, condition and setting of the job very quickly, and can show things a sketch misses, such as rust or a nearby pipe. Its limit is that it gives no sizes unless a tape is in view, and a photo can hide depth and distort shapes. In practice, a good job pack uses a sketch or CAD drawing with sizes, backed up by photos.
markingPoints: Sketch: quick on site (advantage); not to scale, may be unclear (limit)
CAD: accurate, to scale, easy to change (advantage)
CAD: needs equipment, skill and time (limit)
Photo: quick, shows real shape and condition (advantage); no sizes, distortion (limit)
Concludes that they are best used together

essays.stem: You lead a team of four who will make a balcony railing for a guest house in Port Antonio from a drawing. Explain how you would brief the team on the drawing before work starts.
essays.modelAnswer: I gather the team at the bench with the current drawing, the parts list and the job card. I first show them the title block: the drawing number and revision, the scale, the projection method and the units, and I make sure everyone has the same revision. I go through the GA, showing the overall length and height, how the posts, rails and balusters fit, and the fixing details to the balcony. I point out the material and finish notes, for example galvanised or stainless steel because the site is near the sea. I explain the weld symbols on each joint and any site welds. I go over the key tolerances, such as baluster spacing and post positions, and how we will check them. I then give each person their part of the job and the parts they are responsible for, and ask them to explain back what they will make. I invite questions and note anything that needs to go to the supervisor. This makes sure everyone reads the drawing the same way.
markingPoints: Uses the current drawing, parts list and job card; checks the revision
Explains title block items (scale, projection, units)
Explains the GA, materials, finish and weld symbols
Points out key tolerances and how they will be checked
Gives clear tasks and checks understanding (questions, explain back)

practical1.title: Survey a fabricated steel frame and produce a checked sketch set with weld symbols and a cutting list
practical1.brief: As a team, survey a fabricated steel item at the Centre that the assessor chooses (for example a welding bench, a trolley or a gate frame). First plan the survey: the views needed, the tools and who does what. Make a dimensioned freehand orthographic sketch (at least a front view, a plan and an end view, in first angle or the Centre's chosen method) and an isometric sketch, on squared paper, with a title block. Show every member's section size, all key sizes from clear datums, hole positions, and a weld symbol for each type of weld you can see. Then write a cutting list for the item. Each member measures and sketches at least one view or detail, and checks a view drawn by another member. A second team then re-measures five sizes that the assessor picks and records them on your check sheet. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the sketch set, cutting list and check sheet are finished and the area is clean.
materials: A fabricated steel item at the Centre, chosen by the assessor
Steel tape, steel rule, vernier caliper, square and spirit level
A phone or camera for photos
Title block and cutting list blank forms, check sheet
photos: The written survey plan, with who does what
Members measuring the item, with a tape in view
The orthographic sketch with sizes and weld symbols
The check sheet filled in by the second team
checklist: Took part in planning the survey and knew their task
Measured accurately from clear datums and recorded sizes neatly
Drew their view in proportion, in the right projection position
Added correct section sizes, notes and weld symbols
Helped prepare a correct cutting list (sizes and quantities)
Checked another member's view and corrected errors found
Worked safely around the item and left the area tidy
safety: Check the item is stable and isolated if it has any power supply
Wear safety boots; take care of sharp edges and burrs
Keep walkways clear while measuring; do not climb on the item
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Read a fabrication drawing: cutting list, weld schedule, full-size set-out and inspection of a sample frame
practical2.brief: As a team, use the fabrication drawing the assessor gives you (for example a small balcony railing panel or a bracket frame) to prepare the job and check a sample. First, check the drawing: title block, revision, projection, notes and parts list, and write down any queries. Next, make a cutting list and a weld schedule (each joint, its weld type, size and side, from the weld symbols). Then set out one corner joint full size on a steel sheet or board from the drawing, with the members and weld preparation shown. Finally, inspect a sample frame the assessor provides against the drawing: measure the key sizes and diagonals, check the weld sizes with a gauge, and fill in an inspection report saying which sizes pass or fail the tolerance. Each member leads one of the four stages and takes part in the others. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the papers and the set-out are finished and the area is clean.
materials: A fabrication drawing with weld symbols and a parts list (from the assessor)
A sample fabricated frame to inspect
Steel sheet or board for the full-size set-out, marking tools
Steel tape, steel rule, square, fillet weld gauge
Cutting list, weld schedule and inspection report forms, calculator
photos: The drawing check notes and queries
The cutting list and the weld schedule
The full-size set-out of the corner joint
Members measuring the sample frame and its diagonals
A weld being checked with the fillet gauge
checklist: Read the title block, revision, projection and notes correctly
Produced correct cut lengths and quantities from the drawing
Read the weld symbols correctly into the weld schedule
Set out the corner joint full size and accurately
Measured the sample frame correctly and judged each size against the tolerance
Led their stage clearly and supported the other stages
Wrote clear entries in the inspection report
safety: Wear safety boots and gloves when handling the sample frame and steel sheet
Lift the frame with a team lift; support it so it cannot fall
Keep scriber points capped; take care of sharp edges
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
